how-to-choose-which-tax-clients-to-accep.text:
Tax Season Client Picker · guide

How to choose which tax clients to accept late in the season: capacity and deadline math

Short answer: accept the set of engagements whose combined fee, less direct costs, is highest and that you can still finish by their filing or extension deadlines with the hours you really have. Hours before a deadline are the scarce thing, so a well-paid return can be a bad choice if it takes the hours two better ones needed.

A worked queue

Ten late-season engagements, one preparer giving the queue 6 hours of real work per business day. Fees run from $275 for a W-2-only 1040 to $1,400 for a multistate C-corp return that takes 16 hours; each row has the business day it must be done by (the filing or extension deadline). The numbers are illustrative, not typical fees.

  • Accepting requests in the order they arrived fits 4 clients and earns $2,990 net: it takes engagements in arrival order until the larger, better-paying ones no longer fit.
  • Biggest fee first fits 3 clients and earns $3,360: it takes the $1,400 C-corp return and the $1,300 trust return, then adds the amended-return project and has no hours left for anything else.
  • Best net per hour first fits 7 clients and earns $3,278: many small wins that crowd out the two big engagements that pay more together.
  • The best set accepts 5 clients (41 hours) and earns $3,555 net, or $86.71 an hour. That is $195 more than the best simple rule.

Five clients are turned down. The Schedule C 1040 would earn a place at a fee of about $485 (it pays $425), the partnership return at about $810, the C-corp return at about $1,470, the W-2-only 1040 at about $347 and the late-filer catch-up at about $425. Those are the fees to quote those clients instead of the fee on offer.

What to feed it

  1. Hours: the whole engagement, from document intake through preparation, research, review and client questions. Track a few finished returns to calibrate this.
  2. Hours per day: what you can truly give the queue after existing clients, notices, admin and the unexpected.
  3. Direct cost: per-return software or e-file fees, a reviewer's pay, filing fees you absorb. Not your own time.
  4. Due day: business days from today to the filing or extension deadline you are working to, where 1 means the end of today. An extension only moves a deadline if it is filed on time, and it does not extend time to pay.

Check your competence for each return type, your credentials and PTIN or EA authority, due-diligence requirements, Circular 230 and professional standards, and your engagement-letter terms first: some require you to take or decline clients for reasons the arithmetic cannot see, and work you can do competently, with proper due diligence, comes before any optimum. Do not paste taxpayer names or identification numbers; use engagement labels.

Questions

How do I decide which late-season tax clients to accept?

Compare whole queues, not single clients: a set is deliverable when, for every due day, the hours of the engagements due by then fit in the hours you have by then. Of all deliverable sets, the best is the one with the highest total fee less direct cost. The picker finds it exactly for up to 16 engagements.

Is taking the biggest fee first a good rule?

Not reliably. A big engagement often takes the hours two good ones needed before the same deadline. On the worked queue it earns $3,360 against $3,555 for the best set.

What should a client pay to be worth taking?

The picker prints, for each client it turns down, the fee at which the best set would include it. That is the number to quote that client, or the number to quote the next time the same kind of late-season return arrives.

You are responsible for verifying its output, for the numbers you enter, for preparer competence, due diligence and Circular 230 or other professional-standards duties, and for any engagement letter that governs which clients you take. The worked example is illustrative arithmetic, not a forecast.

TAX SEASON CLIENT PICKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Ten late-season clients, one preparer: which should you accept?

Accepting requests as they arrive, or the biggest fee first, fills your last weeks with the wrong returns and leaves the good ones past their deadline. Paste the queue — fee, hours of work, the business day each is due (filing or extension deadline) and what each costs you out of pocket — and get the exact set of engagements with the highest total net that you can still finish on time, the order to work them, the fee each declined client would need to pay, and what first-come acceptance leaves behind.

For independent tax preparers, enrolled agents, bookkeepers and other solo practitioners paid per engagement. Nothing is uploaded: the text box is analysed in this browser and never leaves your device.

    Prefer a CLI?

    Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — reads a file or stdin:

    node cli.mjs plan clients.csv --hours-per-day 6 --booked 4 --booked-due 2 --json
cat clients.csv | node cli.mjs plan - --hours-per-day 7

    Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. More: How to choose which tax clients to accept late in the season: capacity and deadline math.

    What's recognised

    InputHandling

    The plan is exact for the numbers you type (a search over every set of engagements, up to 16). One person and one stream of hours; work is treated as divisible across days, so a return that must be done in one sitting, a client meeting that needs a specific day, a second preparer or reviewer, scope that grows after acceptance, repeat-client value, referral relationships and the cost of declining a client are not modelled. Extension deadlines are only as good as the extension actually being filed on time; penalties and interest are not modelled. Business days are counted by you; weekends and holidays are not.

    Common questions

    Does it upload my client list?

    No. The browser page works on the text you paste (use engagement labels, not client names or taxpayer identification numbers), in your own browser, and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads a local file or stdin and makes no network call.

    How is the best set found?

    Work is divisible across days, so a set of engagements can be delivered on time exactly when, for every due day, the hours of the returns due by then fit in the hours you have by then. The tool searches the engagements in due-date order, abandons a partial set the moment it misses a deadline, and keeps the highest total net. That is the exact best set for the numbers you give, and the tests compare it with trying every subset.

    Why would it turn down a client I would normally take?

    Because hours before a deadline are the scarce thing. A good-paying return can take the hours two other returns needed to hit the same deadline. The tool says what the engagement would need to pay to earn its place, which is the fee to quote that client instead.

    Where do the hours and costs come from?

    From your own records: the hours a typical return of that type takes you from document intake to filing, and the out-of-pocket cost of each engagement. They are your estimates, so treat the plan as a decision aid, not a forecast.

    Who is it for?

    Independent tax preparers, enrolled agents, bookkeepers and other solo practitioners paid a fee per engagement who choose which late-season clients to accept against fixed filing and extension deadlines.
